source_text: Τὸ μὲν οὖν ἄθεοι μὴ εἶναι, ἕνα τὸν ἀγένητον καὶ ἀΐδιον καὶ ἀόρατον καὶ ἀπαθῆ καὶ ἀκατάληπτον καὶ ἀχώρητον, νῷ μόνῳ καὶ λόγῳ καταλαμβανόμενον, φωτὶ καὶ κάλλει καὶ πνεύματι καὶ δυνάμει ἀνεκδιηγήτῳ περιεχόμενον, ὑφ᾿ οὗ γεγένηται τὸ πᾶν διὰ τοῦ αὐτοῦ λόγου καὶ διακεκόσμηται καὶ συγκρατεῖται, θεὸν ἄγοντες, ἱκανῶς μοι δέδεικται. Νοοῦμεν γὰρ καὶ υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ. Καὶ μή μοι γελοῖόν τις νομίσῃ τὸ υἱὸν εἶναι τῷ θεῷ. Οὐ γὰρ ὡς ποιηταὶ μυθοποιοῦσιν, οὐδὲν βελτίους τῶν ἀνθρώπων δεικνῦντες τοὺς θεούς, ἢ περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ πατρὸς ἢ περὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ πεφρονήκαμεν. Ἀλλ᾿ ἔστιν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ λόγος τοῦ πατρὸς ἐν ἰδέᾳ καὶ ἐνεργείᾳ· πρὸς αὐτοῦ γὰρ καὶ δι᾿ αὐτοῦ πάντα ἐγένετο, ἑνὸς ὄντος τοῦ πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ. Ὄντος δὲ τοῦ υἱοῦ ἐν πατρὶ καὶ πατρὸς ἐν υἱῷ, ἑνότητι καὶ δυνάμει πνεύματος, νοῦς καὶ λόγος τοῦ πατρὸς ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ. Εἰ δὲ δι᾿ ὑπερβολὴν συνέσεως σκοπεῖν ὑμῖν ἔπεισιν, ὁ παῖς τί βούλεται, ἐρῶ διὰ βραχέων πρῶτον γέννημα εἶναι τῷ πατρί, οὐχ ὡς γενόμενον (ἐξ ἀρχῆς γὰρ ὁ θεός, νοῦς ἀΐδιος ὤν, εἶχεν αὐτὸς ἐν ἑαυτῷ τὸν λόγον, ἀϊδίως λογικὸς ὤν), ἀλλ᾿ ὡς τῶν ὑλικῶν ξυμπάντων, ἀποίου φύσεως καὶ γῆς ἀχρείας ὑποκειμένων δίκην, μεμιγμένων τῶν παχυμερεστέρων πρὸς τὰ κουφότερα ἐπ᾿ αὐτοῖς, ἰδέα καὶ ἐνέργεια εἶναι προελθών. Συνᾴδει δὲ τῷ λόγῳ καὶ τὸ προφητικὸν πνεῦμα· Κύριος γάρ, φησίν, ἔκτισέ με ἀρχὴν ὁδῶν αὐτοῦ εἰς ἔργα αὐτοῦ. Καίτοι καὶ αὐτὸ τὸ ἐνεργοῦν τοῖς ἐκφωνοῦσι προφητικῶς ἅγιον πνεῦμα ἀπόῤῥοιαν εἶναί φαμεν τοῦ θεοῦ, ἀποῤῥέον καὶ ἐπαναφερόμενον ὡς ἀκτῖνα ἡλίου.Τίς οὖν οὐκ ἂν ἀπορήσαι, λέγοντας θεὸν πατέρα καὶ υἱὸν θεὸν καὶ πνεῦμα ἅγιον, δεικνύντας αὐτῶν καὶ τὴν ἐν τῇ ἑνώσει δύναμιν καὶ τὴν ἐν τῇ τάξει διαίρεσιν, ἀκούσας ἀθέους καλουμένους; Καὶ οὐκ ἐπὶ τούτοις τὸ θεολογικὸν ἡμῶν ἵσταται μέρος· ἀλλὰ καὶ πλῆθος ἀγγέλων καὶ λειτουργῶν φαμεν, οὓς ὁ ποιητὴς καὶ δημιουργὸς κόσμου θεὸς διὰ τοῦ παρ᾿ αὐτοῦ λόγου διένειμε καὶ διέταξε περί τε τὰ στοιχεῖα εἶναι καὶ τοὺς οὐρανοὺς καὶ τὸν κόσμον καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτῷ καὶ τὴν τούτων εὐταξίαν.
pass_a_gloss: That therefore we are not atheists, because we consider one ungenerated and eternal and invisible and impassive and incomprehensible and uncircumscribed, grasped by mind alone and reason, encompassed by light and beauty and spirit and indescribable power, under whom all things have been made through his word and have been adorned and are held together, having been shown to me sufficiently. For we consider also the Son of God. And let no one think it laughable that the Son is of God. For not as poets mythologize, showing the gods to be no better than men, nor have we thought about God and Father or about the Son. But the Son of God is the reason of the Father in idea and in energy; for through him and because of him all things have been made, the Father and the Son being one. And the Son being in the Father and the Father in the Son, by unity and power of spirit, the Son of God is the mind and reason of the Father. And if because of excess of intelligence it seems to you to be examining, what the child wants, I will say briefly that he is the firstborn of the Father, not as having been made (for God, being eternal mind, had the reason in himself from the beginning, being eternally rational), but as the idea and energy have proceeded before the material things, of a simple nature and useless earth having been subjected, the thicker mixed with the thinner upon them. The prophetic spirit also agrees with the reason; for it says, The Lord made me the beginning of his ways for his works. And we say that the holy spirit which energizes in those who speak prophetically is an effluence of God, flowing out and being referred back like a ray of the sun. Who then would not be at a loss, hearing us say God the Father and Son of God and Holy Spirit, showing both their power in unity and their distinction in order, being called atheists? And our theological part is not established on these things; but we also say a multitude of angels and ministers, whom the creator and maker of the world God distributed and ordered through his word with him, concerning the elements and the heavens and the world and the things in it and their good order.

choices.why: refers to those who do not believe in God
refers to Jesus Christ as the son of God
refers to the third person of the Trinity

bible_refs.note: The Lord made me the beginning of his ways for his works

pass_b_english: I have adequately demonstrated that we are not atheists, since we acknowledge one God — ungenerated, eternal, invisible, impassible, incomprehensible, and uncircumscribed — who is apprehended only by mind and reason and encompassed by light, beauty, spirit, and indescribable power, under whom all things came to be through his Word and are ordered and held together. We also recognize the Son of God. Let no one suppose it laughable that God has a Son. Our conception differs entirely from the poets who invent myths, portraying their gods as no better than human beings; we have not thought that way about the Father or the Son. Rather, the Son of God is the Father's Reason in idea and in energy, for through him and by him all things were made, the Father and the Son being one. Since the Son is in the Father and the Father in the Son, united by the unity and power of the Spirit, the Son of God is the Mind and Reason of the Father. If the force of this reasoning compels you to ask what the Son desires, I will answer concisely: he is the Father's firstborn, not as one who came into existence (for God, as eternal Mind, possessed his Reason within himself from the beginning, being eternally rational), but as Idea and Energy that proceeded before all material things, when formless matter and useless earth lay subjected, the denser mingled with the lighter upon it. The prophetic Spirit concurs with this Reason, declaring, "The Lord created me the beginning of his ways for his works" (Proverbs 8:22). We also affirm that the Holy Spirit, who inspires prophetic utterance, is an efflux of God, flowing forth and returning like a ray of the sun. Who would not be perplexed to hear us called atheists when we confess God the Father, God the Son, and the Holy Spirit, displaying both their power in unity and their distinction in order? Our theology does not rest on these points alone; we also teach a multitude of angels and ministers, whom the Creator and Maker of the world, God, distributed and ordered through his Word to govern the elements, the heavens, the world, all that is in it, and their harmonious arrangement.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological distinctions of the Greek text, particularly the distinction between the eternal generation of the Logos and the temporal creation of the material world. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Greek. The scripture citation (Proverbs 8:22) is correctly identified and added in Pass B as required.
